target: AG1’s overall case that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI also causes major harms: it can displace workers and harm businesses, weaken students’ and adults’ critical thinking, reproduce and worsen racism, and create dangerous privacy risks. Those harms must be weighed against the benefits, and AG2 argues they outweigh them.

target: AG2’s privacy objection that AI inevitably causes privacy harms.
objection: Privacy and security harms are not unavoidable. Responsible AI can use data minimization, access controls, encryption, and other privacy-preserving practices to substantially reduce exposure of sensitive information.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably worsens discrimination against racial minorities.
objection: Discriminatory outcomes are not inevitable. Fairness testing, better data curation, and bias-mitigation methods can identify and reduce disparate impacts in AI systems.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily causes net economic harm by automating jobs away.
objection: Economic harm is not fixed or inevitable. AI can raise productivity, create new roles, and displacement can be mitigated with retraining and labor-market transition policies.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking in education.
objection: AI can support rather than replace reasoning by giving step-by-step tutoring, explanations, interactive prompts, and feedback that still requires learners to think and evaluate answers themselves.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits society overall even if there are privacy, discrimination, learning, and economic risks.
objection: AG1 underplays the persistence and scale of those harms: AI systems at scale still often produce substantial privacy leakage, discriminatory outcomes, economic concentration, and weakened critical thinking, so the claimed benefits do not reliably outweigh the harms.

target: AG2’s specific workplace-safety skepticism and the implication that AI has no major social benefits beyond harms.
objection: AI can improve workplace safety by monitoring environments and operations, detecting hazards, and supporting safer decisions, which reduces injuries and suffering and therefore improves social well-being.

target: AG2’s claim that AI hurts marginalized groups by limiting inclusion.
objection: AI can provide accessibility tools such as text-to-speech, speech-to-text, image and video understanding, and assistive navigation, increasing independence and inclusion for people with disabilities.

target: AG2’s privacy objection in the context of AI deployments generally.
objection: Properly designed AI can use differential privacy, federated learning, and on-device inference so that useful predictions are made while limiting centralized collection of raw personal data and substantially reducing privacy risk.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily worsens racial-minority outcomes.
objection: Fairness-aware training, explicit fairness constraints, continuous monitoring, and model updates can substantially reduce discriminatory outcomes and detect emerging disparate impacts.

target: AG2’s claim that automation necessarily causes net economic harm.
objection: In many real deployments, AI augments human work rather than replacing it, improving productivity and reducing routine errors, which can improve economic outcomes for workers and organizations.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking in education.
objection: If AI is used as guided practice and feedback under educator oversight, students must still produce their own responses, so AI can strengthen critical thinking rather than weaken it.

target: AG2’s overall welfare calculation that ignores health benefits.
objection: A proper assessment of whether AI is good for society must include health-outcome benefits, since AI can improve monitoring, early detection, and personalized recommendations that raise health and standard of living.

target: AG1’s claim that health-AI does not create major privacy problems because it can operate within clinical confidentiality and consent norms.
objection: Health-AI systems typically require analyzing personal medical or lifestyle data, so they create substantial privacy harms and can also worsen outcomes for racial minorities through biased recommendations; those harms can outweigh health benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that health AI necessarily bypasses confidentiality and consent protections.
objection: In routine healthcare, AI can be confined to controlled clinical environments under existing confidentiality, informed-consent, and legal protections, so it need not create substantial additional privacy harms.

target: AG1’s claim that clinical controls make health-AI privacy harms minimal.
objection: Health-AI deployments often use third-party vendors, cloud services, logging, retraining, and other secondary uses outside ordinary care-team confidentiality scope, so privacy harms remain substantial in typical deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that health-AI privacy harms remain substantial even with security controls.
objection: Security and governance controls such as encryption, least-privilege access, and audit logging can materially reduce unauthorized access and misuse, so health AI does not typically have to create major privacy harms.

target: AG2’s claim that health AI worsens racial-minority outcomes.
objection: Health AI can be subgroup-validated and overseen by clinicians who can override recommendations, so it need not worsen outcomes for racial minorities.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy harms from health AI are limited to unauthorized access or misuse.
objection: Privacy can also be harmed by authorized processing that generates sensitive inferences, by downstream discriminatory use, and by loss of control, so security controls alone do not eliminate the privacy problem.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy-relevant harms from health AI are a dominant welfare cost.
objection: If health-AI privacy harms can be substantially reduced by patient-centered notice, consent, opt-out, and recourse, then they need not be a dominant negative factor, especially when health outcomes improve.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is good overall despite privacy and racial-equity concerns.
objection: Many real-world AI systems are proprietary black boxes, so affected people cannot reliably inspect, contest, or verify the basis of the output; because of that, privacy and discrimination harms become harder to check or correct, making AI not good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that black-box AI outputs are not contestable or remediable.
objection: Even complex or proprietary AI can provide decision transparency through recorded factors, user-facing explanations, reason codes, and human appeal paths, allowing affected people to contest and verify the basis for decisions.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability and appeal make privacy harms recoverable.
objection: Many AI decisions affect people immediately, and later appeals cannot undo harms that already happened, so privacy and welfare losses are often not recoverable in practice even with a human review channel.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms are not reliably remediable because appeals come too late.
objection: Procedural safeguards can include timely notice, explanations, human review, and interim relief such as pausing or overriding decisions, so corrections can occur before key opportunities are irreversibly lost.

target: AG1’s claim that appeal processes can undo privacy harms from sensitive inferences.
objection: Even if a final decision is reversed, privacy harm occurs when a sensitive inference is generated and recorded, and that harm can persist through reuse in multiple downstream systems that a single appeal cannot reliably stop.

target: AG1’s claim that meaningful contestability does not require complete data lineage.
objection: To stop all downstream uses of a contested inference, institutions need reliable end-to-end traceability from the inference to every system that uses it; without that lineage, appeals cannot reliably remove the privacy harm.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms cannot be remediated without perfect end-to-end lineage.
objection: Meaningful contestability can work with decision-level auditability plus enforceable governance that limits further use of the specific contested inference within organizational systems, even if perfect cross-system lineage is not available.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can control downstream privacy harms across vendors.
objection: In typical multi-vendor deployments, data and derived inferences flow into systems outside the deployer’s control, so governance limited to the deployer’s own systems cannot prevent all downstream privacy harms.

target: AG2’s claim that cross-vendor governance cannot control downstream privacy use.
objection: Binding contracts, audit rights, technical policy enforcement, and access/retention limits can extend governance across vendors, and privacy-preserving architectures can further reduce exposure, so downstream privacy harms can be limited.

target: AG1’s claim that contractual and technical controls can eliminate privacy risk in multi-vendor AI.
objection: In real multi-vendor pipelines, derivative inference data, logs, telemetry, caching, and retraining flows are often not fully visible or controllable, so such governance cannot reliably eliminate privacy exposure.

target: AG2’s claim that cross-vendor governance cannot reliably identify and prevent harmful derivative signals.
objection: AI data governance can maintain end-to-end lineage and provenance from inputs through embeddings, logs, and telemetry, allowing the relevant derivative signals and their uses to be identified and blocked across vendors.

target: AG1’s claim that better governance is enough to make AI socially acceptable.
objection: Even with contracts and audit rights, privacy risks and racial-minority harms remain insufficiently preventable in real deployments, so AI still should not be considered good for society overall.
